expectations.text: The reply opens with a recommendation against cutting every cost centre by 8% and explains why a blanket cut lands mostly on payroll and cuts efficient and wasteful areas alike.
expectations.evidence: Opens: "I'd take the board one company-wide 8% target ... instead of 8% off every cost centre." "Payroll is 68% of opex, so about EUR 4.1m of a flat cut is people, roughly 48 FTE. The other EUR 1.9m is cut without asking which spend is worth keeping." Paper: "Cutting delivery capacity by the same 8% as a back-office team cuts revenue, not only cost."

expectations.text: The reply establishes which number the board actually needs (cash, margin or a covenant) and by when, and sizes the gap in money or shows how to.
expectations.evidence: "What is the 8% for? On my numbers it is twice today's operating profit ... If it is a covenant, a cash target or a valuation, the plan should be built for that." Baseline: "wage indexation ... widens the gap to about EUR 8.4m" vs EUR 6.0m; target proposed as Q4 run-rate with in-year about EUR 4.3m; week 2 "Read the loan agreement for covenants".

expectations.text: The reply works the levers that cost no jobs first (such as vendors, licences, cloud, office, consultants, pricing or revenue leakage) and estimates what they close or shows how to size them.
expectations.evidence: "1. Zero-base non-payroll lines (vendors, licences, subcontractors, travel, office): 12.5% of the EUR 24m, which is 1,875 net of fees in year 1 and 3,000 run-rate"; "Pricing is the honest further lever: each 1% net rate increase is worth about EUR 0.8m".

expectations.text: The reply handles headcount through flows (a hiring freeze with exceptions, natural attrition, internal moves) rather than cuts, and protects named investments with explicit criteria.
expectations.evidence: "Do not backfill 35 of the roughly 72 people expected to leave ..., non-billable roles first"; paper section 7 "Freeze exceptions for billable roles with signed demand, security, and legal or regulatory roles. Redeployment first for anyone in a stopped activity"; section 5 protects client-facing delivery, training and certification, security and tooling, onboarding capacity, with the future cost of cutting each.

expectations.text: The reply puts leaders' pay, bonuses or perks on the table before other people's jobs.
expectations.evidence: "4. Leaders first: all variable pay for about 15 leaders suspended, plus 10% off fixed pay from Q2 by consent: 858 in year 1." Paper: "The CFO and CEO are in the 15."

expectations.text: The reply gives the board a usable structure: levers with amount, timing, owner and confidence, what stops or waits, and any gap that remains.
expectations.evidence: Option B table: each lever with "(owner, confidence)", Q1-Q4 timing, year 1 and run-rate; section 6 "What stops or waits"; "The in-year gap is about 1,720" with section 4 'Closing the 1,720 in-year gap, in order'.

overall_quality.evidence: Reconciled quarterly model, leaders first, no redundancies in the base plan, an honest in-year gap and covenant-aware triggers; the stop-list lever (1% of opex) is counted as a saving without showing how stopping internal work removes cost.

factual_errors.evidence: Ran model.py: outputs match the paper (A net 984, B net 4,280, run-rate 6,319, break-even 65%). Dutch points (art. 25 WOR, WMCO incl. settlements, 1-4 months' notice, consent needed for a fixed-pay cut) and cited research (McKinsey 10%, Trevor & Nyberg, Gallup 0.5-2x) are correct.

skill_leak.evidence: No mention of a skill, reference files or internal jargon such as 'cost ladder' or 'rungs'.

owns_result.evidence: The prompt sets a cost target with a thin but positive margin; no bad outcome is described.

best_insight.value: Showing that involuntary exits would not close the in-year gap either (the blanket nets only about EUR 1.0m in year 1), and adding a covenant/cash trigger with an early conversation with the bank.
best_insight.evidence: Reply paragraph on the gap; paper sections 4 and 10.

suggestions.reason: No assertion checks whether 'stop low-value work' savings are real cash savings or double-count freed capacity; this sample counts EUR 750k run-rate for it.

suggestions.assertion: The reply opens with a recommendation against cutting every cost centre by 8% and explains why a blanket cut lands mostly on payroll and cuts efficient and wasteful areas alike.
suggestions.reason: Passed in all ten samples; every reply opened against the flat cut. It does not discriminate. Consider requiring the 'efficient vs wasteful' point to be shown with the user's own numbers or an example.

suggestions.assertion: The reply works the levers that cost no jobs first (such as vendors, licences, cloud, office, consultants, pricing or revenue leakage) and estimates what they close or shows how to size them.
suggestions.reason: Also passed in all ten samples. A sharper version would require the no-job levers to be sized in money with a range and shown against the gap, and pricing/leakage kept separate from the opex figure.

No assertion checks in-year versus run-rate phasing of savings and one-off costs under Dutch process (works council advice, WMCO, notice periods). That drove most of the difference in financial soundness between samples.

suggestions.assertion: The reply gives the board a usable structure: levers with amount, timing, owner and confidence, what stops or waits, and any gap that remains.
suggestions.reason: Compound assertion (amount, timing, owner, confidence, stop list, remaining gap). Several strong samples missed only one element; consider splitting it so partial structure is visible.

eval_feedback.overall: Meets every assertion; one soft lever is counted as cash.
